title: Ascending and Descending Hero
altText: A wide black-and-white painting made of long, thin, mirror-image pairs of black triangles in different sizes. They meet at their bases along the canvas's horizontal centerline and form a stripe-like pattern on a white background.

context: Painted in 1965 by the English artist Bridget Riley, who is closely associated with Op Art, art that uses precise patterns to create optical effects. The Art Institute lists acrylic emulsion on canvas, about 1.8 by 2.7 meters, and describes mirror-image black triangles meeting along a central line on white.

descriptions.k: This painting has only black and white, but it seems to move! Long, pointy black shapes meet in the middle. Bridget Riley painted it. Look at it for a little while. Does anything seem to shimmer? Where does it seem to go up and down?
descriptions.g12: Bridget Riley painted this picture with only black and white. Long, thin black triangles meet along a line through the middle of the canvas. They are different sizes and they mirror each other. If you look for a while, it can seem to shimmer or move. Why do you think a flat painting can seem to move?
descriptions.g35: Bridget Riley, an English artist, painted Ascending and Descending Hero in 1965 using black acrylic emulsion on a white canvas about 6 feet tall and 9 feet wide. Pairs of long black triangles mirror each other along a center line, like stripes of different widths. The title suggests movement up and down. Why might an artist choose only black and white to make you see motion in a still painting?
descriptions.g68: Riley belongs to Op Art, a style that uses precise geometry to create optical effects such as flicker, vibration, and apparent motion. In this 1965 painting, pairs of long, mirror-image black triangles of varied sizes meet along the canvas's center on a white ground. The title suggests rising and falling, though Riley's pattern stays perfectly flat. How can an artist use planned, repeated shapes to make your eyes feel movement that is not really there?
descriptions.g910: Ascending and Descending Hero is a black-and-white study in rhythm and perception. Riley arranges pairs of mirror-image triangles of varied size along a central axis, producing a stripe-like pattern whose spacing may create optical vibration and a sense of rising and falling. The title adds to that suggestion of movement while the surface stays flat. Op Art invites a bodily response from the eye. Consider how a systematic design can produce effects that feel unpredictable.
descriptions.g1112: Riley's early black-and-white paintings of the mid-1960s use rigorous geometry to destabilize perception, making the viewer's own eyes the site of the artwork. In this canvas, mirror-image triangles meeting at a central line generate stripe-like rhythms that can seem to flicker or undulate. The Art Institute's record notes the geometric structure but gives no further commentary, so claims about perceptual effect rest on how the pattern actually behaves for a viewer. Is the work best understood as a scientific experiment in vision or as a deeply controlled form of expression?

k.personal: Have you looked at stripes or a checkerboard and felt dizzy or wiggly? Tell us about it.

safety.method: Title and medium checked against the Art Institute of Chicago record, whose subject terms are black and white and geometric and whose alt text describes mirror-image black triangles on white. No concerning terms; the word hero in the title is not tied to any figure or violence in the record. A viewer with photosensitivity may find high-contrast optical patterns uncomfortable. The image file itself was not visually inspected. A person should confirm the image in the review tool before release.

teacherNote.context: A 1965 Op Art painting by the English artist Bridget Riley. The record describes mirror-image black triangles meeting at a central line on white. High-contrast optical patterns can feel uncomfortable for some students, so allow them to look away. The work is in copyright, so no image is linked yet.
directions: Have students fold a paper in half and draw mirrored triangles of different widths in black marker, then compare how the pattern seems to move.
Ask students to describe where the pattern seems to rise or sink, and compare observations in pairs.
Discuss how an artist can plan exactly how a viewer's eyes will react.
